title: Custom Water-Cooled 4090 Build
summary: A full tower built for AI work as much as for games. The RTX 4090 runs on a custom open water loop, on a full-cover block fed by its own pump, reservoir and 240 mm radiator. The CPU sits on a separate 240 mm AIO.
specs: CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D 10th Anniversary, 8 cores, 96 MB V-Cache, 105 W
GPU: ASUS TUF RTX 4090 24 GB, on a Bitspower full-cover water block
Motherboard: MSI MAG B550 Tomahawk Max WiFi, AM4 ATX
RAM: 32 GB DDR4-3000, four G.SKILL Ripjaws V sticks at 3000 MT/s on A-XMP
Storage: 1 TB WD SN750 NVMe for Linux, 1 TB Samsung 860 EVO SATA for Windows 11
GPU loop: Bitspower block, pump and reservoir, 240 mm front radiator, push-pull on be quiet! Pure Wings 3 fans
CPU cooler: Cooler Master Elite Liquid 240 AIO, top mounted
PSU: EVGA SuperNOVA 850 G2, 850 W 80+ Gold, fully modular
notes: The 4090 runs on a custom open loop, not a sealed AIO. That means stripping the stock cooler off a card worth more than the rest of the build, mounting a full-cover block, then filling and leak-testing the loop before power ever reaches the board.
The 24 GB of video memory is the reason for this card. A model that fits entirely in it runs on the GPU; a model that does not has to spill into system memory and slows to a crawl.

I sized the cooling for that load. A game pushes the card in bursts, but a training or inference job holds it near full power for hours. Water carries that heat away far better than air, and the card holds its clocks instead of throttling.
Two separate cooling systems share one chassis. The GPU loop takes the 240 mm front radiator in push-pull. The CPU AIO takes the 240 mm top mount, so neither one breathes the other's exhaust.
The machine dual boots. Linux lives on the PCIe 4.0 NVMe drive and carries the AI toolchain, Windows 11 on the SATA SSD for games, on separate disks so neither installer can touch the other.
Four DDR4 sticks on AM4 is the hard case for the memory controller. Two 2x8 GB kits hold 3000 MT/s on A-XMP with all four slots filled.

title: Dual-Chamber Display Build
summary: A top-end build in a HYTE Y70 Touch, around an RTX 5080 and a Ryzen 7 9800X3D. Two screens run inside the case: the cooler reports temperatures and the side panel plays artwork.
specs: Cooling: NZXT Kraken Elite AIO with the round LCD pump head
Airflow: three ARGB fans on the side intake
Case: HYTE Y70 Touch, dual-chamber, wraparound glass with a vertical touchscreen panel
notes: The 9800X3D and the 5080 are a deliberate pairing. The X3D chip is the fastest gaming CPU available, so at any resolution the graphics card stays the limit and the CPU never becomes the bottleneck.
The Y70 is a dual-chamber case. The power supply and every cable run sit in a second compartment behind the board, so the glass corner shows only the parts worth looking at.
The Kraken Elite pump head reports GPU temperature, and the Y70 touchscreen plays artwork chosen for it.
Front-panel wiring and the touchscreen feed both route through the rear chamber, so nothing crosses the window.

title: RTX 4060 Ti Gaming Build
summary: A gaming build on a Ryzen 7 9800X3D and an Aorus RTX 4060 Ti, in a white NZXT tower with the cabling run clean behind the board.
specs: Cooling: NZXT tower cooler, 120 mm fan
Case: white NZXT mid-tower, hex-mesh intake panel
notes: I put the CPU ahead of the card on purpose. A 9800X3D with a 4060 Ti means the graphics card is the limit today, and a card upgrade later lifts the whole machine without touching the platform.
The B650-A is AM5, so the board takes DDR5 and later Ryzen chips on the same socket.
Cable management was its own job. White sleeved extensions reach the board and the card from the closest grommet, so the front of the case stays clean through the glass.
The hex-mesh panel feeds the intake directly, and the tower cooler exhausts straight out the back.

title: Scion FR-S
summary: A Scion FR-S I do the work on myself: suspension, exhaust, wrap and lighting. Same approach as a PC build. Research the part, confirm it fits before ordering, do the job, and find out what actually broke instead of guessing.
notes: Factory headlight housings are sealed. They have to be heated open, fitted with the halo and the projector ring, wired back to a controller, then sealed again tight enough that they never fog. It is the same work as lighting a PC. Plan the runs, hide the wiring, and leave the controller somewhere you can still reach.

The starlight headliner is a few hundred fibre-optic strands fed through the roof lining to one LED engine. The headliner comes down, every strand gets placed and trimmed flush, and the driver has to end up somewhere serviceable.

Coilovers and headers are the mechanical half. Struts come out and go back in to torque spec, ride height gets set, and the car is aligned afterwards. Headers mean working underneath it, on exhaust studs and gaskets, with the oxygen sensors moved over.
I wrapped the car myself. That job is patience more than anything. Trim and lights come off, every panel gets cleaned, and the film goes on without trapping air under it.
All of it carries over to a shop floor. Read the service manual, check fitment before buying, and diagnose the actual fault instead of throwing parts at it.

title: Destiny Dungeon
summary: A text RPG set in the Destiny 2 universe. You sign in with your Bungie.net account, pick one of your real Guardians, and play in a chat window. A large language model runs the story around that Guardian's class, race, Power level and stats.
specs: Model: Llama 3.3 70B Instruct Turbo, served by Together.ai
APIs: Bungie.net REST API, OAuth 2.0 sign-in
World: seven Destiny locations in a JSON data file
notes: Built from the DeepLearning.AI short course Building an AI-Powered Game. The course builds a generic fantasy dungeon on Together.ai and Gradio. I kept the game loop and replaced the invented fantasy world with Destiny 2 and with live data from a real account, because I would rather play in a world I already know.

Most of the design sits in the prompt. Every turn assembles the Destiny lore, the Guardian's class and stats, the current location and the chat history into one prompt, then asks the model for the next beat of the story. Changing that prompt changes how the game plays, so most of the tuning happened there rather than in the game code.

Signing in is real OAuth 2.0 against Bungie.net. The callback runs over HTTPS on localhost with a self-signed certificate, and the tokens are cached and refreshed on disk so later runs skip the browser entirely.
The seven locations sit in locations.json, apart from the code. Adding a place to the world is a data edit, not a code change.
Content moderation is off. The course used LlamaGuard, Together no longer serves it on their serverless API, and the game master prompt holds that line instead.

The inventory stores equipped item hashes rather than names. When a player asks what they are carrying, the model invents plausible Destiny gear instead of reading the real loadout. The fix is a lookup against the Destiny manifest.
Built as a pair project with a working engineer. I wrote most of it.

title: Asteroids
summary: A playable clone of the 1979 arcade game, in Python. Fly a ship, shoot the rocks, and every rock you hit splits into two smaller ones. Built by working through the Boot.dev guided project.
notes: A CircleShape base class holds position, velocity, radius, and the collision check. The ship, the rocks, and the shots all inherit from it, so collision is written once.
Pygame sprite groups handle what updates and what draws. Each class registers its own containers, so the main loop never has to know what kind of object it is holding.
Movement multiplies by delta time, so the ship moves at the same speed no matter what frame rate the machine hits.

Splitting is the part I had to think about. A hit rock spawns two smaller ones, rotated off the original heading by a random 20 to 50 degrees and sped up 20 percent, and the split repeats until the pieces are too small to break.
